Total: 13 periods · 8h 40min

periods.textbook_anchor: How Paper is Made — Students read about Pihu learning that paper comes from trees, including drawing books, newspapers, paper napkins, and chart papers (p. 119)
materials: one sheet of newspaper per student
periods.visual_aids: Textbook figure showing types of paper products

time_bands.activity: Teacher holds up a newspaper and asks: what is this made of? Students share ideas freely. Teacher collects responses on the board without confirming or denying.

Students open Textbook p. 119 and read the story of Pihu discovering that paper comes from trees. Teacher asks: which of the paper things around us right now might have needed a tree to make it? Students point out objects in the classroom.

Whole-class discussion: if paper comes from trees, what does that mean for forests? Students share what they already know or have heard at home about trees being cut. Teacher listens and notes key ideas on the board without correcting yet — the aim is surfacing prior knowledge.

Teacher closes with an open question for students to carry home in their minds: think about one paper object you used today and wonder where the tree for it might have come from. No written homework is set.

periods.implied_lo: Students can connect a manufactured everyday material to its natural source and articulate why that connection matters.
periods.section_context: Paper from trees, drawing books, newspapers, paper napkins, chart papers, Pihu's story, wood pulp requiring large numbers of trees.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students whether their grandparents or elders at home have ever mentioned writing on leaves or cloth — this opens naturally into the section's content about talapatra and palm leaves without labelling it as a special category of knowledge.

periods.textbook_anchor: How Paper is Made — Students collect old newspapers and fenugreek seeds, soak torn newspaper pieces with fenugreek seeds overnight, then blend or mash the soaked mixture into pulp (p. 119)

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks: has anyone ever seen paper being made, or seen what paper looks like before it is a sheet? Brief share-out. Teacher explains that the class will begin making their own paper today.

Students open Textbook p. 119 and read the recycled-paper activity instructions together. Teacher works through each step with the class: tearing newspaper into small pieces, measuring water, adding fenugreek seeds. Students note why fenugreek is used — it acts as a binding material.

In small groups, students tear their newspaper sheets into the smallest pieces they can, place them in bowls with water and fenugreek seeds, and stir the mixture. Teacher circulates, asking groups to describe what they notice about the paper as it absorbs water.

Groups label their bowls with their group name. Teacher explains that the mixture needs time to soak so that the fibres soften — the soaked bowls will be set aside for the next stage of the activity. Students record in their notebooks: what materials we used and why we used each one.

periods.implied_lo: Students can carry out the initial steps of a multi-step material-transformation process and explain the purpose of each ingredient used.
periods.section_context: Old newspapers, fenugreek seeds (methi) as binding material, water, soaking process, paper pulp preparation.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: While students are tearing paper, ask: does anyone's family use fenugreek seeds in cooking or medicine? This surfaces how a familiar household item plays a different role here, grounding the inquiry in local knowledge without making it a separate episode.

periods.activity_title: Making Recycled Paper — Rolling and Drying
periods.textbook_anchor: How Paper is Made — Students spread the blended pulp on a flat base, roll it into thin sheets, and leave it to dry (p. 119)
materials: Soaked newspaper-and-fenugreek pulp from each group's bowl

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly recaps the pulp-preparation steps that students carried out — soaking, fenugreek seeds as binder — by asking groups to describe what happened to their newspaper pieces. Students observe that the paper has softened and the fibres have separated.

Students open Textbook p. 119 and re-read the rolling and drying steps. Groups then spread their pulp onto flat boards, pressing it out with their hands first and then rolling with a rolling pin or bottle to form a thin, even sheet.

Students press old cloth pieces onto the sheet to absorb excess water, then carefully lift the boards and place them in a well-ventilated spot to dry. Teacher asks each group: is your sheet even everywhere? What happens if it is too thick in one place?

While sheets dry, students record in their notebooks: what the pulp looked and felt like before rolling, and what they predict the dried sheet will look and feel like. Teacher draws out the concept that paper-making is essentially separating and re-bonding fibres.

periods.implied_lo: Students can execute the forming and drying stages of a material-transformation process and predict how a material's properties change as it moves through processing steps.
periods.section_context: Pulp spreading, rolling into thin sheets, pressing with cloth, drying, fibre bonding in paper-making.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students: if our sheet is too thin in some places, what might that tell us about how commercial paper factories try to make every sheet the same? This connects the hands-on challenge to the scale of industrial production without leaving the activity.

periods.activity_title: Natural Colour Experiment on Recycled Paper
periods.textbook_anchor: How Paper is Made — Students cut recycled paper into equal-sized pieces, apply different natural ingredients in equal quantities, and record colour and brightness observations in the table (p. 120)
materials: Dried recycled paper sheets (or plain white paper if sheets are not yet dry)
natural colouring ingredients: turmeric, beetroot juice, spinach leaf, henna, flower petals

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the idea that dyes can be made from plant parts — leaf, flower, root, seed, stem — and asks: have you seen your family use turmeric or beetroot to colour food or cloth? Students share examples.

Students open Textbook p. 120 and read the natural colour experiment instructions. Each group cuts paper into equal-sized pieces and sets up their ingredients in small bowls, making sure the quantity of each ingredient is the same for a fair comparison.

Students apply one ingredient to each piece of paper and observe: what colour does it produce? How bright is it? They fill in the observation table on Textbook p. 120, recording the colour and their assessment of its brightness for each ingredient.

Groups share their most interesting finding with the class. Teacher asks: which plant part gave the strongest colour? Why might people have used these dyes on cloth and pots before factory dyes existed? Students note their answer in their notebooks.

periods.implied_lo: Students can conduct a controlled comparison of natural materials, record observations systematically, and draw a conclusion about which variable produced the strongest outcome.
periods.section_context: Natural dyes from plant parts (leaf, flower, root, seed, stem), turmeric, beetroot juice, spinach, henna, flower petals, equal-quantity comparison, colouring on recycled paper.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students whether anyone has seen block printing, tie-dye, or fabric colouring done at home or in a local workshop — this brings the natural-dye tradition into the room as lived knowledge rather than historical fact.

periods.textbook_anchor: How Paper is Made — Students make a greeting card, a paper mask, or another item from their recycled paper (p. 121)
materials: natural-dyed paper pieces from the previous experiment

time_bands.activity: Teacher shows Textbook p. 121 and asks students to choose what they will make — a greeting card, a paper mask, or another item of their choice that uses their recycled paper. Students briefly plan their item in two sentences in their notebooks.

Students create their chosen item using recycled paper, natural-dyed pieces, and available materials. Teacher circulates, asking each student: what design choice did you make, and why? Students are encouraged to use the natural-coloured pieces as part of their decoration.

A quick gallery walk: students place their finished items on their desks and move around to look at two or three other creations. They note one thing they notice about how someone else used the recycled paper differently from themselves.

Teacher asks: if you could make this item again, what would you do differently? One or two students share. Teacher connects the activity to the idea that making useful or beautiful things from waste paper is one way to reduce the need for new paper.

periods.implied_lo: Students can design and construct a functional or decorative object from a recycled material, demonstrating that waste materials have creative potential.
periods.section_context: Greeting card, paper mask, recycled paper as creative material, natural-dyed paper pieces, making useful or decorative objects from waste.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: If students mention rangoli, kite-making, or festival decoration traditions that use paper or natural colours, invite them to describe these briefly — this enriches the creative session with local context without derailing the making task.

periods.textbook_anchor: How Paper is Made — Students discuss whether we waste paper and how we can reduce that wastage (p. 122)

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens Textbook p. 122 and poses the first discussion question aloud: do you think we waste paper? Students think quietly for a moment, then share examples from their own day — homework sheets, paper cups, torn notebook pages. Teacher lists examples on the board.

Teacher poses the second question from Textbook p. 122: how can we reduce wastage of paper? Students brainstorm in pairs and then share with the class. Teacher groups the suggestions on the board under rough headings — use less, use again, make something new — without yet naming the 5Rs.

Teacher asks students to look at the list on the board and reflect: which of these changes do you already make at home? Which one would be the easiest to start? Students write two sentences in their notebooks: one thing they already do, one thing they will try.

Teacher closes by connecting the discussion to the paper-making work: the students now know how much effort — soaking, mashing, rolling, drying — goes into making even one sheet. Ask: does knowing this change how you feel about wasting paper? One or two students respond aloud.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify specific paper-wasting behaviours in their own lives and propose concrete actions to reduce that waste.
periods.section_context: Paper wastage in daily life, reducing wastage, using both sides, paper cups, torn notebook pages, connection between effort of making and responsibility of using.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: If students mention that older family members scold them for wasting paper or wrap purchases in newspaper, use this as an entry point — these household habits are the lived version of the reduce-and-reuse idea the section develops.

periods.textbook_anchor: Making Responsible Choices — Students discuss the 5Rs situations table (Maya, Rohan, Sara, Kabir, Priya, shopkeeper) and write which R each situation belongs to (p. 125)

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the 5Rs — Refuse, Reduce, Reuse, Repurpose, Recycle — writing each word on the board with a one-phrase example. Students repeat each R and its example aloud to build familiarity with the vocabulary.

Students open Textbook p. 125 and read the six situations (Maya, Rohan, Sara, Kabir, Priya, shopkeeper). In pairs, they discuss which R each situation belongs to and write their answers. Teacher circulates and listens, noting where pairs disagree — these are the productive moments to use in the whole-class discussion.

Whole-class share-out: teacher goes through each situation, inviting pairs to give their answer and their reason. Where there is disagreement, teacher opens it to the class: which R fits better, and why? Students revise their written answers if they change their minds.

Teacher asks: can you think of one situation from your own home or neighbourhood that fits one of the 5Rs? Two or three students share. Teacher notes that the 5Rs are not just rules in a book — they are choices people already make every day.

periods.implied_lo: Students can classify real-life waste-management behaviours into a named framework and justify their classification with a reason.
periods.section_context: 5Rs (Refuse, Reduce, Reuse, Repurpose, Recycle), Maya not using a plastic straw, Rohan using blank pages, Sara giving old books, Kabir painting an old bottle, Priya cutting old clothes, shopkeeper making paper envelopes.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students whether their family has a habit of saving and reusing old newspapers, glass jars, or cloth bags — this connects the formal 5Rs vocabulary to practices students may have grown up with, making the framework feel like naming something already known.

periods.activity_title: Braille and the 5Rs — Widening the Circle
periods.textbook_anchor: Making Responsible Choices — Students learn about the Braille system as a specialised use of embossed paper enabling visually challenged people to read and write (p. 125)
materials: a sheet of thick paper per student for tactile exploration
periods.visual_aids: Textbook figure showing Braille script if present

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks: we have talked about paper as something we read, write on, and recycle — but has anyone thought about how a person who cannot see reads? Students share prior knowledge or guesses freely.

Students open Textbook p. 125 and read about the Braille system. Teacher explains that Braille uses raised dots pressed into thick paper so that readers feel the text with their fingertips. Each student takes a sheet of thick paper and uses a pencil tip to press small dot patterns gently — experiencing what it might feel like to create raised marks.

Teacher poses a connecting question: Braille books use a great deal of thick paper. How might the 5Rs apply to Braille materials — can they be reduced, reused, or repurposed? Students discuss in small groups and share ideas. Teacher steers toward: reducing waste matters for everyone, but solutions may look different for different users.

Brief reflection: teacher asks students to write one sentence in their notebooks — what did learning about Braille add to their thinking about paper and its uses? Two or three students read their sentences aloud.

periods.implied_lo: Students can connect a specialised use of a common material to the broader principle of inclusive and responsible resource use.
periods.section_context: Braille system, embossed paper, raised dots, reading and writing for visually challenged people, connection to 5Rs and responsible paper use.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: If any student has a family member or knows someone who uses Braille or other assistive tools, invite a brief share — this centres inclusion as lived experience rather than a textbook concept.

periods.activity_title: Paper Toys and Decorations — Repurposing in Action
periods.section_ref: Let Us Get Creative with Paper
periods.textbook_anchor: Let Us Get Creative with Paper — Students transform old and used paper into toys and decorative items such as newspaper figures, paper fans, and decorative birds (p. 126)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 126 showing newspaper figures, paper fans, decorative birds

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens Textbook p. 126 and shows the examples: newspaper figures, paper fans, decorative birds. Teacher asks: which R from the 5Rs does making a toy from old newspaper belong to? Students identify Repurpose and explain why — giving an object a new purpose, not just using it again.

Students choose one item to make — a paper fan, a newspaper figure, or a decorative bird — using only old newspapers and used paper. Teacher demonstrates the first fold or step for each option so that all students can begin independently. Students work individually or in pairs.

Students display their finished items on their desks. Teacher asks two or three students to describe the steps they used: what did you start with, what did you do first, what was the hardest part? This verbal walk-through consolidates the process.

Teacher closes with the question: if every class in the school made one paper toy each week from old newspapers, how might that affect how much new paper the school needs? Students share a quick thought each.

periods.implied_lo: Students can transform a discarded material into a functional or decorative object and identify which waste-management principle their action demonstrates.
periods.section_context: Newspaper figures, paper fans, decorative birds, old and used newspaper, Repurpose principle in action.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students whether paper fans, kites, or newspaper boats are made at home or in their neighbourhood for festivals or play — this surfaces local craft traditions embedded in the repurpose idea without presenting them as separate content.

periods.activity_title: Reflecting on Paper Pulp Objects and Personal 5Rs Commitments
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students write what objects can be made from paper pulp, asking teachers and elders for ideas, and write one step they can take for each of the 5Rs (p. 127)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads aloud from Textbook p. 127: what are some objects you can make using paper pulp? Students brainstorm — egg cartons, bowls, papier-mâché masks, pots, trays — and teacher lists these on the board. Teacher encourages students to think of things they have seen elders make.

Students write their answers to the first reflect task in Textbook p. 127 in their notebooks, adding at least one idea they learned from home or from the class brainstorm. Teacher circulates and prompts students who are stuck with: what would a bowl made of paper pulp feel like? Where have you seen something like that?

Students open Textbook p. 127 and complete the second reflect task: writing one personal step for each of the five Rs — Refuse, Reduce, Reuse, Repurpose, Recycle. Teacher reminds students that these should be real, small actions they can actually take, not general statements.
Two or three students share one of their five commitments aloud. Teacher asks the class: is there an R that feels harder to practise? Why? Brief discussion closes the unit.

periods.implied_lo: Students can generate concrete personal action steps for each element of a named waste-reduction framework and connect those steps to real changes in their daily behaviour.
periods.section_context: Objects made from paper pulp (egg cartons, bowls, papier-mâché, pots, trays), 5Rs personal commitments (one step per R: Refuse, Reduce, Reuse, Repurpose, Recycle).
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt students to ask a family elder — grandparent, neighbour, or local craftsperson — what they remember about objects made from paper pulp or recycled material; this brings inter-generational knowledge into the reflection without requiring a formal homework task.

periods.activity_title: Discussing Daily Changes for Paper Conservation
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students discuss changes they can bring in daily life using the 5Rs rule to avoid paper wastage and complete the table with their ideas (p. 127)

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens Textbook p. 127 and reads the final reflect task aloud: discuss the changes you can bring in your daily life using the 5Rs rule to avoid wastage of paper. Students recall what the 5Rs are by naming them without looking — teacher confirms on the board.

In small groups, students discuss the ideas table on Textbook p. 127, filling in each row with a concrete daily-life change. Teacher circulates, asking groups: is this something you could actually do? Is it something your family already does?

Each group shares one idea from their table that the class has not heard yet. Teacher builds a collective list on the board. Where students give similar ideas, teacher asks: is there a way to make this more specific to your own home or school?

Students write a two-sentence personal reflection in their notebooks: the one change from today's discussion they are most likely to make, and why that one feels possible. No mark or grade is attached — this is a personal note.

periods.implied_lo: Students can propose specific, feasible changes to their own daily routines that reduce paper waste, drawing on a structured discussion with peers.
periods.section_context: Daily-life changes using 5Rs, paper wastage avoidance, ideas table completion, group discussion of feasible personal actions.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask groups whether any idea in their table is something a family member or elder already does without calling it an R — naming familiar habits as examples of Refuse or Reuse helps students see conservation as part of their existing culture, not an external imposition.

periods.activity_title: Observing and Classifying Types of Paper
periods.section_ref: Different Types of Paper and their Uses
periods.textbook_anchor: Different Types of Paper and their Uses — Students observe writing paper, newspaper, art paper, cardboard, and tissue paper, paste small pieces in their books, and write each type's uses (p. 123)
materials: Small pieces of writing paper, newspaper, art paper, cardboard, tissue paper (one set per student or pair)

time_bands.activity: Teacher places all five paper types on a desk at the front and asks students to come look, touch, and describe what they notice without naming the types yet. Students use words like thin, rough, stiff, soft, shiny — teacher writes these describing words on the board.

Students open Textbook p. 123 and read the activity instructions. Each student or pair receives one set of paper samples. They paste a small piece of each type into their notebook, then write the name and at least one use beside each piece, guided by Textbook p. 123.

Students feel each sample again and record one physical property for each: tissue paper is thin, soft, and absorbent; cardboard is thick and hard. Teacher asks: why does a box need to be made from cardboard and not tissue paper? Students reason from the property to the purpose.

Teacher poses a closing question: which type of paper uses the most trees to make — and which might use the fewest? Students share ideas, connecting the observation activity to the chapter's broader theme of natural resource use.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe and record the physical properties of different paper types and explain how those properties make each type suited to a specific use.
periods.section_context: Writing paper, newspaper, art paper, cardboard, tissue paper — properties (thin, soft, absorbent, thick, hard) and uses (writing, wrapping, boxes, art, cleaning).
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students whether their family reuses any of these paper types — for example, wrapping food in newspaper, saving cardboard boxes, or using newspaper as a surface for art — this surfaces everyday observation as valid data alongside the textbook activity.

periods.activity_title: From Tree to Choice — A Whole-Chapter Synthesis
periods.textbook_anchor: How Paper is Made — Students read about Pihu learning that paper comes from trees, including drawing books, newspapers, paper napkins, and chart papers (p. 119)
materials: one sheet of any paper type per student

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws a simple journey line on the board: TREE → WOOD PULP → PAPER SHEET → PAPER PRODUCT → WASTE. Students contribute what they know about each stage — the trees needed, the water and energy used, the fenugreek binding in recycled paper, the natural dyes that colour it. Teacher fills the line with the class's collective knowledge.

Teacher poses: at which point on this journey can a person make a responsible choice? Students identify every stage — choosing to use less, reusing a bag, repurposing newspaper, recycling — and connect each to one of the 5Rs. Teacher writes the Rs beside the relevant stages on the journey line.

Students look at the paper sheet in front of them and write in their notebooks: three things this one sheet of paper required to exist (from natural resources, from human processes, or from cultural knowledge — e.g. palm-leaf writing, natural dyes, banana fibre as an alternative). They then write one responsible choice they will make about this kind of paper.

Two or three students read their written reflections aloud. Teacher closes by noting that the chapter's ideas — paper from trees, natural dyes, historical writing materials, the 5Rs, different paper types, and Braille — are all part of one question: how do humans make things, and how do they make those choices well?

periods.implied_lo: Students can trace a material from its natural source through processing and use to responsible disposal, applying multiple concepts from across the chapter to construct a joined-up understanding.
periods.section_context: Full chapter synthesis: paper from trees, wood pulp, fenugreek binding, natural dyes, talapatra and palm leaves, banana fibre, 5Rs (Refuse, Reduce, Reuse, Repurpose, Recycle), different paper types and properties, Braille, responsible daily choices.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: This unit draws the whole chapter together — invite students to name any concept or material from any part of the chapter that they found surprising or that changed how they think about paper; this surfaces the chapter's range without requiring a formal recap sequence.

coverage_handoff.section_context: Full chapter synthesis: paper from trees, wood pulp, fenugreek binding, natural dyes, talapatra and palm leaves, banana fibre, 5Rs (Refuse, Reduce, Reuse, Repurpose, Recycle), different paper types and properties, Braille, responsible daily choices.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: How Paper is Made — Students read about Pihu learning that paper comes from trees, including drawing books, newspapers, paper napkins, and chart papers (p. 119)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Whole-chapter synthesis: students build a journey line from tree to waste, map the 5Rs onto it, write a three-fact reflection on one sheet of paper, and discuss the chapter's unifying question about how humans make things well.

assessment_items.question_text: Pihu learns that drawing books, newspapers, and paper napkins are all made from trees. Which of the following statements best explains why this matters?

options.label: A
options.text: Making paper uses large numbers of trees, water, and energy, so each sheet of paper has a cost to the environment.

options.label: B
options.text: Only newspapers are made from trees; other paper products use different materials.

options.label: C
options.text: Paper is made from water, not from trees, so forests are not affected.

options.label: D
options.text: Trees grow very quickly, so cutting them for paper does not cause any problem.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is A. This tests whether the student read and engaged with the core claim of the section — that all common paper products share a single natural source with real environmental costs.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can connect a manufactured everyday material to its natural source and articulate why that connection matters.

competency.competency_text: Describes usage of natural resources in their immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.D: Student holds the misconception that trees are a rapidly renewable resource and that paper production is therefore harmless — a common prior belief that the section directly challenges.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student has confused water (used in the paper-making process) with the primary raw material, misreading or skimming the section's opening explanation.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student has partially retained only one example (newspaper) and failed to generalise the section's core claim to all paper products.

assessment_items.question_text: When making recycled paper at home, fenugreek seeds (methi) are added to the soaked newspaper. What is the purpose of fenugreek seeds in this process? Give one reason.
expected_elements: Fenugreek seeds act as a binding material (they hold the paper fibres together).
Without a binder, the pulp would not hold its shape when rolled and dried.
assessment_items.annotation: A complete response names the binding function. Accept any wording that conveys 'holds the fibres together' or 'helps the sheet stay in one piece'. Do not require the word 'binder' — the concept is what matters.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can carry out the initial steps of a multi-step material-transformation process and explain the purpose of each ingredient used.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: Fenugreek seeds act as a binding material — they hold the paper fibres together.
The binding function allows the pulp to form a coherent sheet that can be rolled and dried without falling apart.

assessment_items.question_text: After the newspaper pulp is spread on a flat board and rolled into a thin sheet, what happens to the paper fibres as the sheet dries? Describe what you would expect the dried sheet to look and feel like compared to the wet pulp.
expected_elements: As the sheet dries, the water evaporates and the fibres bond together.
The dried sheet is flat, firmer, and holds its shape — unlike the wet pulp which was soft and shapeless.
The dried sheet can be written or drawn on, showing that the fibres have formed a usable surface.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept descriptions that correctly contrast wet pulp (soft, shapeless, wet) with dried sheet (firm, flat, holds shape). The student need not use the word 'bond' — look for evidence that they understood the transformation.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can execute the forming and drying stages of a material-transformation process and predict how a material's properties change as it moves through processing steps.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: Water evaporates during drying, causing fibres to come together and bond.
The dried sheet is flat, firmer, and holds a definite shape — contrasting with the soft, wet pulp.
The surface of the dried sheet can be written or drawn on.

assessment_items.question_text: In the natural colour experiment, a student applied turmeric, beetroot juice, spinach leaf, and henna to equal-sized pieces of recycled paper, using the same quantity of each. Why was it important to use the same quantity of each ingredient?

options.label: A
options.text: Because all natural ingredients produce the same colour when used in the same quantity.

options.label: B
options.text: Because the paper pieces absorb exactly one fixed amount of liquid and no more.

options.label: C
options.text: To make sure the comparison is fair, so that any difference in colour is due to the ingredient and not the amount used.

options.label: D
options.text: To save materials, since using less of each ingredient costs the school less money.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is A. This tests whether the student understood the controlled-comparison design of the experiment, which the textbook instruction explicitly required.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can conduct a controlled comparison of natural materials, record observations systematically, and draw a conclusion about which variable produced the strongest outcome.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student misunderstood the purpose of equal quantities, thinking the rule produces uniform results rather than fair comparison — a confusion between controlling a variable and equating outcomes.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student has rationalised the equal-quantity rule as an economic concern rather than a methodological one, showing limited engagement with the inquiry rationale.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student believes paper has a fixed absorption limit, which is a factual misconception about paper properties unrelated to the experiment's design principle.

assessment_items.task: Using your recycled paper (or any available paper), design and make a small greeting card or paper mask. On the back of your creation, write two sentences: (1) what material you used, and (2) why using recycled or waste paper for this item is better for the environment than buying a new card or mask.
assessment_items.scaffold: My creation is a _________. I made it using _________. Using recycled paper for this is better for the environment because _________.
format_of_output: A hand-made greeting card or paper mask
Two written sentences on the reverse
assessment_items.annotation: Assess both the physical creation (is it a deliberate, completed object made from recycled or waste paper?) and the written sentences (do they name the material correctly and give an environment-related reason?). Accept any reasonable environment-reason — saving trees, reducing waste, avoiding new resource use — as correct.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can design and construct a functional or decorative object from a recycled material, demonstrating that waste materials have creative potential.

competency.competency_text: Uses local materials to create simple objects (family tree, envelopes, origami animals) on their own for display or use in classroom processes

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student can intentionally use a recycled or waste material to produce a usable or decorative object, and can articulate the environmental rationale for doing so.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold guides students to name their creation, their material, and their environmental reason — look for all three elements being present even if briefly expressed.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: a completed object that is recognisably a card or mask, made from recycled/waste paper, with two clear sentences naming the material and giving a specific environmental reason (e.g. 'saves trees' or 'stops paper going to landfill'). Weak: an incomplete object, or sentences that repeat the task instruction without adding a genuine reason.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who struggle with writing may dictate their two sentences to the teacher or draw a labelled diagram showing the material used and a symbol for the environment benefit. Students without recycled paper may use any available used paper or the back of a used worksheet.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The creation-plus-explanation format mirrors the chapter's activity structure: making is paired with understanding why the making matters, matching C-1.5's emphasis on objects for display or classroom use.

assessment_items.task: Think about the paper you use in school in one day — notebooks, worksheets, paper cups, scrap paper. Choose two of these and write: (1) one way you currently waste that paper, and (2) one specific thing you will do differently to reduce that waste.
assessment_items.scaffold: Paper item 1: _________. How I waste it: _________. What I will do differently: _________. Paper item 2: _________. How I waste it: _________. What I will do differently: _________.
format_of_output: Written responses for two paper items, each with a wastage behaviour and a proposed change
assessment_items.annotation: Look for honesty in naming an actual wastage behaviour (not a generic statement) and specificity in the proposed change (not just 'I will not waste' but a named action). Both items must be paper products the student actually uses.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify specific paper-wasting behaviours in their own lives and propose concrete actions to reduce that waste.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates how natural resources can be shared, maintained, and conserved (trees, use of rainwater, benefits of millets)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student can honestly identify their own resource-wasting behaviours and convert that recognition into a named, feasible conservation action.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Each of the two items needs three parts: the paper item named, the specific wastage described, and the specific change proposed. A response that fills all six slots with genuine content is complete.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: names real, specific behaviours ('I tear out pages I don't use from my notebook') and specific changes ('I will use both sides before tearing any page'). Weak: generic statements ('I waste paper sometimes' / 'I will be careful') that do not name a real behaviour or a real action.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who cannot write fully may draw the two items and annotate with a word or phrase for each. The teacher may scribe for students with writing difficulties.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Written self-reflection using a structured scaffold
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: Self-reflection on personal behaviour is the intended mode of this section — the scaffold ensures the reflection is specific and actionable rather than aspirational only.

assessment_items.question_text: Kabir has an old glass bottle. Instead of throwing it away, he paints it and uses it as a flower vase. Which of the 5Rs does Kabir's action belong to?

options.label: A
options.text: Recycle — he has broken the bottle down into raw material to make something new.

options.label: B
options.text: Refuse — he has chosen not to accept the bottle in the first place.

options.label: C
options.text: Repurpose — he has given the bottle a new use that is different from its original purpose.

options.label: D
options.text: Reuse — he is using the bottle again for the same purpose it was designed for.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is A. This is one of the six situations from Textbook p. 125. The key distinction being tested is Repurpose (new use, same object) versus Reuse (same use, same object) versus Recycle (breaks down to raw material).
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can classify real-life waste-management behaviours into a named framework and justify their classification with a reason.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates how natural resources can be shared, maintained, and conserved (trees, use of rainwater, benefits of millets)

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student confuses Repurpose with Recycle — they have not grasped that recycling involves breaking a material down into raw material, while repurposing keeps the object intact and gives it a new role.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student confuses Repurpose with Reuse — they have not attended to the fact that the bottle's new use (flower vase) is different from its original use (holding liquid for drinking), which is the defining feature of Repurpose.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student misunderstands Refuse — Refuse means declining to take or use a disposable item in the first place, not deciding not to throw something away.

assessment_items.question_text: The Braille system allows visually challenged people to read and write using raised dots on thick paper. Thinking about the 5Rs of waste management, explain how responsible paper use is important for Braille users and what one R might look like in practice for Braille materials.
look_for: Student correctly identifies that Braille uses thick, specialised paper and that this paper is a resource worth conserving.

Student connects at least one specific R to a Braille-related practice — for example, Reuse (passing Braille books to another reader), Reduce (using digital Braille readers where available), or Repurpose (using one side for Braille and another for a different purpose).
Student shows awareness that responsible resource use matters for all users, including those with different needs, without framing inclusion as an exception.
assessment_items.annotation: This item assesses whether the student can extend the 5Rs principle beyond the most obvious paper contexts to a specialised, inclusion-linked use. Accept any well-reasoned R application. Do not penalise students who name an R that is less obvious — reward the quality of reasoning.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can connect a specialised use of a common material to the broader principle of inclusive and responsible resource use.

competency.competency_text: Learns about basic social and behavioural norms, values, and dispositions that benefit our social and natural environments and that help our society function smoothly (using dustbins, standing in queues, conserving water, using public transportation, keeping one's environment clean, always helping others in need regardless of background)

look_for: Correct identification that Braille uses thick, specialised paper — a resource with its own environmental cost.

At least one specific R applied meaningfully to Braille materials: e.g. Reuse (sharing Braille books between readers), Reduce (using fewer printed pages by going digital where possible), Repurpose (using a Braille sheet's blank side for another purpose).
Recognition that the principle of responsible resource use applies equally to all people, regardless of whether they use standard or specialised materials — no 'exception' framing.

assessment_items.task: Using only old newspapers available in the classroom, make one of the following: a paper fan, a newspaper figure, or a decorative bird. When you have finished, write the name of the item you made and the R from the 5Rs that your action best represents. Write one sentence explaining why.
assessment_items.scaffold: I made a _________. This is an example of _________ (write the R). This is because _________.
format_of_output: A completed paper object made from old newspaper
Three written lines: item name, the R, and a one-sentence reason
assessment_items.annotation: Assess whether the object is completed and made from old newspaper. Assess whether the student correctly identifies Repurpose (the most accurate R for this action) and gives a reason that explains why the newspaper has been given a new purpose. Accept Recycle if the student gives a well-reasoned explanation — but prompt them to consider whether the newspaper has been broken into raw material or given a new form.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Let Us Get Creative with Paper
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can transform a discarded material into a functional or decorative object and identify which waste-management principle their action demonstrates.

competency.competency_text: Uses local materials to create simple objects (family tree, envelopes, origami animals) on their own for display or use in classroom processes

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student can independently create an object from a locally available discarded material and articulate the waste-management principle their action embodies.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Three slots must be filled: the item name, the correct R (Repurpose is the target answer), and a one-sentence reason. The reason must connect the newspaper's original use to its new use as a toy or decoration.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: a completed, recognisable object made entirely from newspaper; correctly identifies Repurpose; reason says something like 'the newspaper was used for reading before but now it has a new purpose as a fan/figure/bird'. Weak: an incomplete object; or identifies Recycle without reasoning; or reason simply restates the R without explaining it.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find folding difficult may tear and paste newspaper into a simpler flat design — the creation principle is the same. Students may work in pairs if motor skills are a barrier, as long as each student writes their own three lines.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The chapter's creative section is explicitly about making — the task mirrors the section's design and adds the conceptual layer of naming the R, linking creation to the waste-management framework.

assessment_items.task: Write one personal action step for each of the 5Rs in the boxes below. Each step must be something you can actually do at home or in school — not a general rule, but a real action you will take.
assessment_items.scaffold: Refuse: I will _________. Reduce: I will _________. Reuse: I will _________. Repurpose: I will _________. Recycle: I will _________.
format_of_output: Five written action statements, one per R
assessment_items.annotation: Assess specificity and feasibility — each statement should name a concrete action ('I will use both sides of every notebook page before starting a new one') rather than a general aspiration ('I will not waste'). All five Rs must be addressed. Accept any valid action for each R.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can generate concrete personal action steps for each element of a named waste-reduction framework and connect those steps to real changes in their daily behaviour.

competency.competency_text: Learns about basic social and behavioural norms, values, and dispositions that benefit our social and natural environments and that help our society function smoothly (using dustbins, standing in queues, conserving water, using public transportation, keeping one's environment clean, always helping others in need regardless of background)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student can translate the 5Rs framework into five distinct, personally feasible behavioural commitments rather than abstract statements.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Five slots, one per R. A complete response fills all five with actions that are specific (name what will be done), first-person (I will…), and feasible (something a Grade IV student can actually do at home or in school).
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: each R has a different, specific action — e.g. Refuse: 'I will not take a paper cup at the water cooler'; Reduce: 'I will write on both sides of every page'; Reuse: 'I will use my old notebook covers for new notebooks'; Repurpose: 'I will make envelopes from old newspaper'; Recycle: 'I will put paper waste in the recycling bin at school'. Weak: repeated or interchangeable statements, or aspirational statements without a named action.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who cannot write full sentences may draw a symbol or image for each R's action and add a word label. The teacher may scribe for students with writing difficulties.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Written personal commitment using a structured scaffold
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The reflect section of the chapter explicitly asks for one step per R — this item mirrors that task directly, testing whether the student can produce what the section designed them to produce.

assessment_items.question_text: Your class has been discussing how to avoid wasting paper in daily life using the 5Rs rule. A classmate says: 'Recycling is enough — we don't need to Refuse or Reduce.' Do you agree or disagree? Give two reasons to support your answer.
look_for: Student takes a clear position (most likely disagreement) and maintains it across both reasons.
At least one reason addresses why Refuse or Reduce matters independently — e.g. recycling still uses energy and water; not taking an item in the first place prevents waste from ever being created.
At least one reason uses specific examples from the chapter or daily life (paper cups, notebook pages, single-use paper) rather than generic statements.
assessment_items.annotation: This is an evaluative item — reward quality of reasoning over agreement with a 'right' position. A student who argues that recycling is enough but supports this with a well-reasoned argument about local recycling infrastructure may receive partial credit. The target position is disagreement, supported by the chapter's content.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can propose specific, feasible changes to their own daily routines that reduce paper waste, drawing on a structured discussion with peers.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates how natural resources can be shared, maintained, and conserved (trees, use of rainwater, benefits of millets)

look_for: A clear position stated at the start of the response.

A reason that explains why Refuse or Reduce is independently valuable — e.g. refusing a paper cup means no waste is created at all, which is better than recycling it later; reducing use means fewer trees are cut even before recycling enters the picture.
A reason grounded in a specific example from the chapter or the student's daily experience — not a general claim like 'recycling is not good enough'.

assessment_items.question_text: A student needs to wrap a heavy book as a gift. She has the following types of paper available: writing paper, tissue paper, newspaper, cardboard, and art paper. Which type of paper would be most suitable for wrapping a heavy book, and why?

options.label: A
options.text: Cardboard — it is thick and hard, so it will protect the book and hold the wrapping in place.

options.label: B
options.text: Newspaper — it already has pictures and words on it, which makes it look decorative.

options.label: C
options.text: Tissue paper — it is soft and thin, which makes it easy to fold neatly around the book.

options.label: D
options.text: Writing paper — it is smooth and clean, which is best for wrapping a gift.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is A. This tests whether the student can apply the property–purpose relationship from the observation activity: cardboard's thickness and hardness make it suited to protecting and supporting a heavy object.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Different Types of Paper and their Uses
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe and record the physical properties of different paper types and explain how those properties make each type suited to a specific use.

competency.competency_text: Describes usage of natural resources in their immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.C: Student chose tissue paper based on ease of folding — a practical concern — rather than matching the material's property (thinness, weakness) to the task demand (protecting a heavy book). This reveals incomplete transfer from property to purpose.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student chose writing paper based on aesthetic quality (smooth and clean) rather than the structural property needed. They may have attended only to appearance rather than function.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student chose newspaper based on a decorative quality (existing print) rather than any structural property, showing that they have not connected the observation of paper properties to the selection of the right paper for a given purpose.

assessment_items.question_text: Trace the journey of a single sheet of paper from the tree in a forest to a piece of waste lying on a classroom floor. At each stage of the journey, name one responsible choice a person could make to reduce harm to the environment. Use ideas from across the whole chapter in your answer.
look_for: Student identifies at least three distinct stages in the paper's journey (e.g. tree → wood pulp → sheet → paper product → waste) and does not conflate them.

A responsible choice is named at each stage and is matched to that stage — e.g. at the tree stage: choosing alternatives like banana fibre or recycled pulp; at the use stage: using both sides; at the waste stage: repurposing or recycling.

Student draws on at least two distinct ideas from across the chapter — for example, combining knowledge of raw materials (trees, water, energy) with the 5Rs and paper-type properties or historical writing materials (talapatra, cloth, palm leaves).
The response is coherent as a journey — stages follow a logical sequence from natural source to waste.
assessment_items.annotation: This is the synthesis item. Award the highest marks to responses that connect multiple chapter ideas coherently across a logical sequence. A response that names all five 5Rs without connecting them to the journey stages is weaker than one that names three stages with well-matched choices. Accept any historically or environmentally accurate reference to alternative materials.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can trace a material from its natural source through processing and use to responsible disposal, applying multiple concepts from across the chapter to construct a joined-up understanding.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates how natural resources can be shared, maintained, and conserved (trees, use of rainwater, benefits of millets)

look_for: At least three distinct, correctly sequenced stages of the paper's journey from natural source to waste.

A responsible choice named at each stage that is logically matched to that stage: e.g. tree stage → use banana fibre or recycled pulp as an alternative; processing stage → use less water and energy; use stage → write on both sides, refuse unnecessary paper; waste stage → repurpose or recycle.

Integration of at least two ideas from different parts of the chapter — e.g. raw-material knowledge combined with the 5Rs; or natural dyes and alternatives like palm leaves combined with paper-type properties.
A coherent narrative structure in which stages follow naturally from one to the next.
